  "summary": "S1 — Fact: deliver a small Python HTTP service in which organisers create events with seat counts and people reserve seats. Fact: the repository is empty; this intake implements nothing. Assumption: the source checkout is the delivery target because no deployment target is named; in an isolated run it remains at its snapshot until final return, and a deployed outcome exists only after release. Discovery must inspect the workspace and any available team documentation for runtime facilities, conventions, owners, and the meanings of organiser, event, seat, and reservation; these are source hints, not verified facts. Open interaction and state questions: discovery should first establish what the runtime provides and any existing product conventions; absent evidence, record defaults of unauthenticated callers, no shared state beyond one running service process, state lasting until that process ends, and no private fields or hidden data. These defaults block persistent or cross-instance reservations, actor verification, and privacy guarantees unless discovery finds support for them. Discovery must also establish reservation rules, including capacity and concurrent requests; absent evidence, default to preventing reservations beyond capacity, with the exact HTTP interface and error responses chosen during delivery. S2 — Fact: include tests covering the service outcomes; discovery should first establish available Python tooling, and otherwise record a standard-library test-tool default. Fact: no person is available during the run; person-only decisions remain open, but the recorded defaults allow work to proceed. Authority is limited to the requested service and tests; no external release target is specified."
